Many will claim that this is like playing the next version of Uplink since it is the most realistic hacking type game since Uplink was released. A very cult genre I think with very few games making a significant mark. I cannot claim to have played that classic so I will have to describe this entertaining game called Hacknet without any past comparisons. I will say that the reason it is compared though is because it takes the hacking seriously and isn't just some casual hacking game for the masses. 

Hacknet has almost no graphics (Maybe about 5 image files in the entire game), it has no video. It is only you looking at a computer screen full of numbers and files. You are a hacker, not Rambo, or James Bond, or Batman. You don't shoot at criminals and punch clowns in the face to save the day. You are a hacker that has found yourself in the middle of some hacking factions that may have stumbled into something big. You get some simple clues at the start that something is going on, but as you delve deeper into the hacking world, get recruited by more skillful hacking groups, and find more mysterious actions going on in your hacking exploits you will get asked to help find out what happened to a popular hacker that has gone missing. Just like everything in the hacking community, all useful information is hidden on systems which need to be hacked into. While looking for that information you will uncover many more secrets as you figure out exactly what happened. A final ending that could be considered a "shock". Very intriguing storyline and way to tell a story all through computer documents, e-mails, IRC chats, etc. 

While the tutorials, and the game itself is friendly to those who have no experience entering command lines, or hacking at all, it may not exactly be for the most casual of gamers. If you are a VERY slow typist you may have some issues when it comes to hacking into computers here in the time frames that are allowed. They have made it easier for you by allowing you to hit "TAB" in certain places to have the game auto-complete command lines if there is nothing else that has the exact same characters and you are in the proper place to do so, however. It absolutely helps to have some typing speed, or at least the knowledge of where all the keys on the keyboard are without having to search them out all the time though. You will have issues if you are THAT slow.  

You are tasked with finding various tools to run .exe files allowing you to open up ports on the computers you hack before running a PortHack program to get access to its files. Some computers early on are very easy to hack with only having to open 1-2 ports, but as you find more tools you may have to open as many as 5 ports, break through a firewall, and get through a proxy all on the same PC while avoiding a tracer too! So it becomes a bit quicker later on where you must know the commands and how to crack the security of various systems as the game progresses while fighting a clock too. You should pick up these skills as you play, but the knowledge of how to access certain databases will require a bit more thought at times. This is where the game adds a bit of strategy and puzzling into the mix. You need to think about what you are trying to do, search through maybe several other computers not just tools, but possibly passwords to OTHER computers, and even find ways to crack encrypted files! So it isn't always completely straightforward with the game holding your hand to get what you need. You will absolutely need to think somewhat critically here to reach your goals. IT is very refreshing to find a game that doesn't just offer you solutions on a silver platter and challenges you to figure things out yourself. It is quite rewarding in some cases to find a solution after thinking all your options through. Sometimes you can even find solutions to future problems by just HACKING into things you aren't even supposed to be working on for no other reason than because you felt like it. 

Hacknet had a few bugs when I got it at release, but it appears that most have been taken care of. I finished the game, but I had a quest that didn't trigger properly so I had to hack my way around into other things to find the info I needed to proceed. Something that really wasn't that big a deal because it felt like I was actually doing something I figured out myself to get around a problem. The triggers have been patched now though as far as I know. Other than that nothing I ran into. 

Hacknet does make you feel like a hacker if you have never done any hacking before in your life. It does use real world terminology and command lines to satisfy those that have in the past too so it isn't just for the hacker n00bs out there. The fast paced and tech-y music playing in the background was designed to make you feel like you are hacking systems as a hero in a movie. Punching in commands as fast you can can before getting caught is definitely helped by the pace of the music playing while you are trying to look into the dirty secrets of every computer you hack into. 

I found Hacknet to be a fantastic feeling of hacking and mystery solving. While you may feel that the middle gets a little bit repetitive when it comes to the hacking, it does usually change up enough in what you need to use to keep the pacing OK. Usually what you find in the files, and of course the ending was payoff enough to continue through if you start to feel like you are staring at a flashing screen too long. I absolutely would not recommend this game to a casual gamer at all. Unlike say a point and click adventure, the puzzles you solve here will require quick thinking and quick fingers at times. Most players will be fine with this, but this is a game that require MUCH more activity on the keyboard than it does with a mouse. So you are typing commands for what you need to do in, and not using a mouse to solve puzzles as much. If you don't read the help files, the tutorial, and look at the academic databases in the game you will not be able to figure things out. If you want a brainless game this one is not for you.

The game has trading cards of course and Steam Achievements, which should be fairly easy to 100% if you can get through the game. This game should take you anywhere from 5-10 hours. More if you look ar ound some and find every secret I suspect.

NOTE: Something I didn't talk about, because I am unsure what it consists of, is that Hacknet will be releasing a patch at some point that includes not just Steam Workshop to add more player made "questing", but it will also have Multiplayer! Like I said I don't know much about those aspects, but they are definitely coming. MP was in the game before Steam so it already exists, but the developers didn't feel it was working well enough yet to release with the Steam release. They wanted to stamp out any single player bugs first before bringing in these other features.

Just... bad. For anyone remotely familiar with computers, this game is cringe-worthy at best. Some weird mix of unix and dos idioms that just don't exist anywhere. The shell is half-assed and inconsistent, and absolutely nothing even closely emulates the real tools which have had their names disgraced. This game might be decent if the file system behaved the way it should, but it does not. In particular:
- wildcards do not work in all commands
- there is no file management beyond rm, mv, and a unicorn scp? can't make directories or copy files on localhost
- devs don't appear to understand how file systems work: ~ and / are used interchangably through the game/tutorial/help docs
- cd can't evaluate more than one step up or down the file tree

some other things to note:
- connections to other systems just don't make sense
- cracking ssh is somehow easier/less resource intensive than screwing with an ftp server? what?
- cat to read files?? really? I smell cat abuse
- no echo?

try again... or don't?

Terribly disappointed by this game. Even the 3€ something during the most recent sale were too much, imho.

While the Game does use some Linux command line inputs to navigate on the computer (cd to change folders, ls to list contents, cat to read a file), those become useless once you completed the tutorial and gain access to the User Interface (mouse control), which is much faster.
"Hacking" works by starting skripts that automate the whole process. All you have to do is start the same 5 skripts by typing their name:
If there is a proxy active, use your own to overload it (click the overwhelm button).
If there is a firewall active, type analyze 5 times, then type solve and the password that was just revealed.
For any available port, type the name of the corresponding skript, wait for it to finish (about 10 seconds), then start the next one.
Sometimes, there is a time limit that never really got close to bothering me.

The story is either really weak or did not really start by the time I quit. You get a first E-Mail (I don't know you, please help me). Then, to build up your skills, you hack at least two dozen systems, always using the method described above, working your way up in some hacker organization you don't really know anything about. When you finally find that you are done with them, you start at bottom level of the next organization.

Conclusion:
Apart from my desire not to leave the game unfinished, there is absolutely nothing that would make me keep playing. Not recommended.

This might just be the 10 years since launch, or my actual experience with computers, but the gameplay loop feels a bit off (pun not intended) for me. The tutorial got me curious enough with the plot to get through, but there is no substance in the base game. Haven't played the DLC, not interested.

If you are into looking at hacker-looking interfaces and typing the same half a dozen commands over and over (tab complete and up key for history available), you will enjoy it. If you want anything that is anymore puzzling than following clear instructions, look elsewhere.

Basically: 1- open an email, 2- click email attachments for a target IP and maybe add a mission summary note to the screen, 3- click a button to connect to said IP and click another button to Probe the system, 4- run the same 2-5 commands on the same list of ports, 5- browse the filesystem to either find or place a file at mostly the same folders, 6- erase all logs and disconnect, 7- repeat. That's it. The game has a simplified terminal emulator missing a few basic features but fine, you can mostly use it to get things done instead of the GUI except when emailing (mostly). There are no puzzles, the exploits are literal executables you run and wait, the only variability is whether the target machine has proxies or a firewall then you gotta login into a bunch of places you already hacked first and run a shell overload (run and wait) then run a firewall analyzer to unscramble a keyword (run and read). Sometimes you gotta disconnect before a tracing timer runs out, which is never an issue until a single mission has like a 3 seconds timer but same difference. If you do *somehow* get traced, you might need to do the one different thing and change your IP address by... following steps 1 through 6! Or just reboot. Yeah, that's it: steps 1-7, sprinkle disconnects according to timer and if something fails just reboot and resume as usual is the whole game. There are two routes if you accept an optional mission but rest assured, same gameplay eveywhere.

Ever wondered what it’s like to be a hacker? Hacknet puts you in the role of one, simulating a realistic command-line hacking experience where you’ll breach systems, retrieve and delete files, cover your tracks, and complete secretive missions—all from a simulated computer interface.

This all depends on how good you are at puzzles, what knowledge you have of computer commands, and how fast you type. If you're an achievement hunter, this will require at least two playthroughs to unlock all the achievements.

[u]AI[/u]
I'm not too sure if this counts as AI, but if you start to hack a really secure place, there's a chance you'll start to get traced. You have ninety seconds to finish up (and for some reason those 'ninety seconds' always go at a different speed) or else you have another minute or so to change your IP. Also, you can reply to emails and kill a guy or two but they don't really count as AI. Not in this game, anyway.

This game will make you feel like a true hacker. Opening the ports of a secure server has never been easier with the programmes and knowledge you have! Firewalls? Not a problem! Proxy? [spoiler]If you write "OpenCDTray" then it will open your actual computer's CD tray if you have one. Pretty damn cool![/spoiler]

Well, it's a computer desktop. Not much else to say. Deep into the game, you can get a theme changer, which changes your desktop in-game. That's about it, really.

The soundtrack is not bad at all. It fits the game and can actually be quite relaxing! Although, you'll probably hear your keyboard half the time. Good stuff!

[u]Overall[/u]
I'd recommend this game to pretty much anyone. Especially those who love puzzle games, like me. This has a great story, challenging puzzles at times, and a great end. The achievements aren't too hard, but they're not too easy. Pick this up if you can, definitely worth €10.

review_text_raw:
*Got the game for $2.99 during a sale*

Hacknet is an interesting game. Let's just get that out of the way. Its got a very good storyline and, while I have some experience in [strike]hacking[/strike] computer security, I didn't find (most) of the puzzles too difficult for the average person to solve. It sets a very good pace, picking up the difficulty very well. I'm writing this review just after completing the game, which took me just over 6 hours.

You start off with a message from Bit, telling you how to use the Hacknet software, etc. etc. Basically a tutorial on how to use it, the command line, that sort of thing. (If you're a linux user, this game will be much easier, the commands are basically the same for navigating the terminal and the like) After this, you're sent off to a hacker group, Entropy. You do a few hacks, and things start to pick up. You rise to the top (naturally) and start going off, investigating. I'd say more but I don't want to risk spoilers. The ending was very intriguing, and worth the effort.

The challenges are similar, but I never got bored of them. Find server at X IP, break down any proxies, firewalls, and open ports to use the almighty PortHack and get the admin password. Then, do whatever you need to, be it uploading or downloading a file, deleting stuff, or (later) even messing with databases and some... other devices. ([spoiler]a pacemaker[/spoiler]) They become more difficult as you progress, adding tracers that initiate an IP change failsafe if you take too long, more ports to open, and more complex firewalls and proxies. You'll need to grab passwords from emails and circumvent servers with powerful tracers, and even more interesting events. The only randomly difficult challenge that jumped me was an attack on my PC, which I was able to avoid using a [spoiler]trap shell[/spoiler]. If it gets you, there is a guide to help you out.

The interface is very intuitive and I never had any unreasonable issues with it, aside from becoming stuck when entering a password I didn't want to enter. (Which is my fault, I clicked login. What did I expect?) Later, you get the option to switch your layout, but none of them are really terrible. You have the terminal window (for commands), the display window (for showing the filesystem, passwords, databases, emails, etc.), the RAM window (watch this one, especially later when you get more RAM-hungry programs), and your NetMap (showing all the IPs you've connected to/can connect to).

The playtime was a good length. I would have liked it to be a bit longer but 6 hours is longer than AAA campaigns. God I hate AAA companies. Be innovative. Or I'll use Hacknet to take down your servers. /rant. Anyway, I'm not complaining about the length. As I said earlier, it never got repetitive, it was always interesting. There was always a sense of "oh gotta do this quickly or they're gonna catch me with that trace" that pushes you forward. Because of that speed though, don't play this game if you're not a quick typist. I have a speed of about 70 WPM (Faster now), which is well above average. I'd recommend being able to go above 40 WPM to play this effectively. 

------------------------------------------------------

Of course, what's a review without a pro/con list.

Pros:
+Good, interesting gameplay
+Active modding community (for extra levels and whatnot)
+Great value for the price (Yes, I know I got it for $2.99. But it's worth the full $9.99)
+Nice visuals (watch out, 1 looks like lowercase L. Tripped me up once)
+Easter Egg bash.org quotes
+Amazing soundtrack. Reflects the mood and urgency of the situations. 10/10 on that.

Neutrals:
+-Console window pops up behind game (Alt Tabbing is a little wierd)
+-Can't skip ending credits

Cons:
-You need to be a quick and accurate typist
-Requires some prior knowledge of terminal commands in order to be efficient (from the start)

------------------------------------------------------

TL; DR

Very interesting, non-repetitive gameplay and a good storyline. Visuals are of high quality and the soundtrack is amazing. However, to be good at this game you should be good at typing ( >40 WPM) and know how to navigate the Linux terminal, or at least pick up on it quickly. (I mean, it's just ls, cd, cat, and mv really) Also, bash.org quotes.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
UPDATE
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

I've just finished the Hacknet: Labyrinths DLC. I'm adding a short little note here about that.

Definetely worth it. Took an extra 3 and a half hours or so to complete, so pretty decent playtime. Much more interesing puzzles than the base game. You are tasked with completing the "Kaguya Trials" from the CSEC list, and join with a group of 3 other hackers. You'll take missions from a list and complete them with the help of the others. While you usually never actually interact with them other than seeing them in the IRC, it does feel like they're helping you. (I won't spoil how, but it becomes apparent in the endgame.) The challenges were a bit more difficult, but nothing that wasn't impossible. A mission towards the end just becomes a cat-and-mouse chase for a password, but while it didn't seem to guide you it wasn't that difficult to follow the clues. Overall, I'd highly rate the DLC. If you have the extra cash when buying Hacknet, I would recommend purchasing it. Do complete it after the main game though, or your NetMap will become a mess...

------------------------------------------------------

TL; DR

Very well done game and a great expansion to the original. I would definitely recommend purchasing this alongside the base game. Just... Play it after you beat the base game.

It took me so long to realise that I was supposed to open up a shell on my own PC, which, if crashed, would somehow take down a proxy server hosted elsewhere? I was assuming I had to find some kind of initial access mechanism to bypass the proxy and execute shellcode on the target PC, but, uh, I guess crashing the equivalent of cmd.exe on my computer really is the future of hacking.

The story is okay, I guess. At least it was easy to 100%.

My advice to anyone interested in a hacking-type game aimed at beginners is to check out the (free!) OverTheWire Bandit wargame, instead; it's fun, and it'll actually teach you something useful.

This is a great hacking game that uses command prompts in order to do things. The game begins with you receiving an email via a Dead Man Switch, which is something that is sent if certain conditions are met(or not), such as not turning on your computer for a week. You can explore the various computers you come across in your travels, read the various text documents that can contain story related content, whether it be main quest or side quest, or joke texts. The side quests are required to a fair degree, as Bits messages wont tell you more until your skill improves by going up in rank on these Organizations. It's not just randomly generated quests like in Uplink, where the differences in quests was basically names and numbers. All of Hacknets Side Quests/Missions have little stories, and as you do these contracts, you may end up finding text documents that hint at what happened to Bit.

For the actual gameplay, it starts out simple, with a few programs to help break through security You'll find more programs to help you get into more complicated systems. 

Now for how Hacknet is different from Uplink. For one thing, there's no upgrades. You can find hacking programs, but there's no upgrading, no hacking store to buy hacking upgrades/software. There's no money actually, and no upgrading your computer. Instead of grinding money to get a more powerful PC and just bulldoze your way through security in Uplink, you need to use your programs and computer more strategically.

This DOSE lower replay value compared to Uplink. In Uplink there's plenty of things to buy and upgrade, and unlimited, if not plain, missions to do. Hacknet is more story driven, with it's main story and the little side stories filled with interesting jobs, info, chat logs, and lots of other things.

I'm not sure how far I am exactly, but at the very least, there's about 35+ side quests at the very least. So there's plenty to do in this game, along with Easter eggs and subtle references to entertain you.

While Uplink was more mouse driven in how you hack, Hacknet is almost entirely with keyboard commands, like Spencer's Hacker Evolution games(The first 2, not the shitty Duality). There is some mouse controls, such as using the mouse to quickly move through a computers directories.

If you like Uplink, you will definitely like Hacknet. If you're interested in hacking games, but haven't played one before, this COULD be a good start, as the difficulty curve is very fair, but Uplink might be better for a newbie.

Btw, you can use the TAB key to auto complete words/directories/programs names. Useful for when you need to quickly break through many ports.

review_text_raw:
[i]Note: I am biased because of the nature of my job. While not related to IT Security, it involves technical troubleshooting / problem solving and all kind of investigations. Basically, less fun version of Hacknet.[/i]

[h3]Accurate Hacking Simulator?[/h3]

I was not exposed to a lot of hacking in games, maybe just a bit in Sleeping Dogs, or Cyberpunk 2077. While other games focus purely on hacking vibes, those tend to ignore the actual process. And Hacknet pays much more attention to the realistic aspect of the game.

Of course, to me it looks like huge oversimplification, but that was made as a game, right? It was made to be simple, fun and accessible. And it never felt like I am working, it felt like I am playing a game and having a good time. So while not being accurate, it nails the realistic hacking experience to enough extent. 

[h3]Handholding or Exploration?[/h3]

The first 60% to 70% percent of the game felt like a tutorial. Fun, with a lot of stories and action, but with a huge sense that I am playing in a sandbox. Everything is pretty safe, and you get what you need to do right from the email, so you need to execute specific steps without much investigation. Yes, you need to look for something specific, but it is usually very algorithmic and follows the same steps. 

So, this feels like handholding to me, and having to "detective" part to it, where you just don't know where to look at and have to think and explore. 

But! There are endgame quests, such as the main story line or Project Junebug quest. Those actually did things perfectly as I have wanted. There is more to reading, investigating, searching and connecting pieces of information together. This was perfect. 

Example: usually it would be "find a (file / password / IP) or edit / remove something. Here is the server.". That is straightforward. 

Project Junebug: Here is the name of the person. Kill him. 

You see what I mean? That is perfect example of what I wanted this game to be. And it eventually has things that appeal to me! So, overall, great experience. Right?

[h3]A bit of so-so moments[/h3]

Just one. The game has netMap, a graph that displays the machines you have connected to. And the graph grows, and there is less and less space, it all  becomes cluttered at some point. And there is no way to clean it up, resize, organize or alter. And this is sad a bit, because the missions that I liked involve a lot of research, but the research progress was hevily impacted by overall messy navigation system. 

But it's a minor thing. What else?


[h3]The Easter Eggs and Secrets[/h3]

While the big part of the game feels like a tutorial, it has a lot of things to explore. Jokes and memes, hidden quests with high rewards - it's all there. So if you want, you can take much more from the game than it offers at a first sight.

Like in some RPGs you can even get overpowered pretty early - if you follow some clues in the game, you can get CLOCK.EXE, which makes game itself hacked. Things that are hidden and require exploration definitely cool here.

[h3]The Music[/h3]

I pay a lot of attention to game OSTs, it makes me love the game more if the music resonates with me. And back in 2017 when I have bought the game, I learned about Hacknet from Remi (The Algorithm) - one of the musicians behind the OST, and I bought it. So, to me the OST is perfectly fitting the game. Just very neat, I thought. Until the final mission.

I have three examples of getting goosebumps from the music in the game:
1. One optional boss fight in Baldur's Gate 3
2. Expedition 33 in various places.

And... Yeah, the final mission of Hacknet! Putting [spoiler]Carpenter Brut's Roller Mobster[/spoiler], one of my favorite synthwave / darksynth tracks ever made me freeze for a minute in awe. And then realize that time is ticking and I need to do everything fast. Perfect sense of adrenaline. Great choice for OST!

[h3]Really solid hacking-lite experience[/h3]

Overall, I liked this game. Relatively short, but never gets dull. And I have not even touched the DLC yet - and it has 97% positive rating! So, while the main game is over for me, I will get to Labyrinths in future to feel this enjoyment again.

It's a good hacking simulation game, but I couldn't bring myself to like it. The game is short, probably will take around 6 hours to finish. The mission objectives were very unclear, I had to use a guide to finish the game. The NetMap was really horrible, everything was cluttered, and it was so hard to use. I couldn't understand the story much. The contract missions felt repetitive for me. Sometimes hacking a PC doesn't save the credentials and I had to hack the same PC multiple times even when looking at my mailbox. About 90% of time, you'll be writing 'Shell, Porthack, Analyze, SSHcrack, FTPbounce' etc. And on top of that you're given just a measly 800 MB ram PC... are you kidding me???

Looking on the bright side, there're definitely plenty of surprises in the game. I mean for real. I used a guide, so it was ruined for me. You'll definitely get stuck at some point of the game. The visual effects were really good. The music went well with the game.
